clue.text: End-to-end and not a walkover

parts.note: a close is an end, as in the close of the day
a finish is an end, as of a race or a piece of work

explanation.surface: A contest that went the full distance from one end to the other and was never one-sided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End-to-end' tells you to set two words for 'end' side by side, the first before the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight result decided at the last moment is the opposite of an easy, one-sided win.

clue.text: One's smothered by fat land-owner

indicators.note: something smothered is covered over on all sides, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: lard is pig fat used in cooking
the Roman numeral for one is I; the 's stands for 'is' and gives no letter

explanation.surface: An overweight property owner who has someone pinned beneath him.
explanation.walkthrough: A LAIRD is a Scottish landowner with an estate, a word worth knowing for non-British solvers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland the owner of a large estate is traditionally called by this title.

clue.text: They'd start growth in recessed ground when no longer cold

indicators.note: ground is the past tense of grind, so the letters are crushed and reformed
these words say the letter for cold has gone from the word before the anagram is made

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Something about growth starting in sunken earth once the chill has lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when no longer cold' takes C out of RECESSED, leaving REESSED, which 'ground' rearranges. 'Ground' looks like soil but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Machines or people that sow seed are what get plants growing in the first place.

clue.text: Incitement from prince reported

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we want the sound of the name

parts.note: Philip is a prince's name, most famously the late Duke of Edinburgh

explanation.surface: A provocation that came from a royal, as told by the press.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Philip was the husband of Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: A stimulus or boost that spurs someone on is a spur to action.

clue.text: Headless individual gambles with believers in alternative stuff

indicators.note: with its head removed, the word for individual loses its opening letter

parts.note: one is a single individual
wagers are bets or gambles

explanation.surface: A decapitated person placing bets alongside fans of crystals and horoscopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of the 1970s-onwards spiritual movement embrace crystals, astrology and similar alternative practices.

clue.text: Brownies and pastries cooked with no end of farina

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters are prepared afresh in a new arrangement
with no says a letter is taken away from the anagram fodder
the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A bakery tray of brownies and pastries made without the last of the flour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of farina' is A, taken from PASTRIES by 'with no' to leave PSTRIES, which 'cooked' rearranges. The baking picture hides that Brownies here are goblins.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore a brownie is a helpful household goblin, a kind of small elf or fairy.

clue.text: Glided most amazingly to overshadow everyone? Could be me

definitions.text: Glided most amazingly to overshadow everyone? Could be me

indicators.note: to overshadow is to loom over and cover, so the rearranged letters wrap around another piece
amazingly suggests the letters are thrown into astonishing disorder

parts.note: all means everyone

explanation.surface: A figure skater boasting that their stunning gliding outshone the whole field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amazingly' rearranges GLIDED MOST into GOLDMEDIST, which 'to overshadow' wraps around ALL. The whole clue is the champion speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: The skater who glides best and beats every rival wins first place at the Olympics.

clue.text: Agent who's bitter in in a case of sickness made up

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another
the case of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

parts.note: bitter is a type of British beer, an ale

indicators.note: in a down clue, up turns the word so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: per means in a or for each, as in miles per hour

explanation.surface: A resentful man struck down with illness who invented things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made up' reverses in this down clue only the piece it governs. Bitter is a British pale beer, and 'a' as 'per' is the sense in 'ten pounds a head'.
explanation.definitionFit: A travelling seller who represents a firm is that company's commercial agent.

clue.text: What the middle-aged can gain from parts of magazines

definitions.meaning: a thickening waist around the stomach, the middle-age spread, read as a spread in the centre
the double pages across the middle of a magazine, often for pictures

explanation.surface: Older readers getting something from sections of their periodicals.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses rest on spread: the paunch of later life and the double page in the middle of a magazine.

clue.text: Hardy perhaps but not right colour

indicators.note: but not says a letter is left out of the word before it

parts.note: Oliver Hardy was the larger half of the comedy duo Laurel and Hardy; perhaps marks him as one Hardy among others

explanation.surface: Thomas Hardy, maybe, but not quite the right shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like the novelist Thomas Hardy but is the comedian Oliver Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull yellowish green named after the fruit is a shade in the paint chart.

clue.text: Type not for the high court?

definitions.text: Type not for the high court?

parts.words: Type not for the high court?
parts.note: read as a court that is not high but lower; in printing, small letters as opposed to capitals

explanation.surface: Asks which kind of person is unfit for a senior judicial bench.
explanation.walkthrough: Type is printing letters, not a sort of person; the small letters were kept in the lower tray of a compositor's case.
explanation.definitionFit: Small letters, not capitals, were stored in the bottom tray of a printer's type case.

clue.text: Extraordinary cuts both sides in dispute call staggering

indicators.note: cuts means pushes into, so this piece goes between the letters around it
both sides of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: odd means strange or extraordinary
to ring is to call on the telephone

explanation.surface: An unusual ruling that splits a quarrel down the middle and brings an astonishing outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staggering' wants to mean astonishing, but here it means tottering, unsteady on one's feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Old and shaky on one's feet, an unsteady walker totters along.

clue.text: Job in a daily newspaper

definitions.meaning: a job is slang for a crime such as a robbery, as in an inside job

explanation.surface: A position advertised in the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The FT is the Financial Times, a London daily business paper; THE FT read as words names it.
explanation.definitionFit: A crime of stealing is called a job in slang, and split in two the letters name the London financial daily.

clue.text: Amigos aplenty not entirely back in city on Mexican border

indicators.note: back means the letters are read from right to left
not entirely says only part of the words is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Plenty of friends, in Spanish, almost returning to a frontier town.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'amigOS APLEnty' and reads backwards. El Paso is in Texas, facing Ciudad Juarez.
explanation.definitionFit: The Texas city sits on the Rio Grande opposite Ciudad Juarez, right at the frontier.

clue.text: Cask in short surrounded by vegetables and flowers

indicators.note: something surrounded by another has that other on both sides of it

parts.note: peas are green vegetables
a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

indicators.note: short means the word is cut, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A barrel briefly ringed by greens and blossoms in a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts the word 'in' to its first letter; that and the cask go between the vegetable's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: These are colourful garden bedding plants with trumpet-shaped blooms.

clue.text: Keep pimm's at first on ice

indicators.note: at first picks the opening letter of the word

parts.note: reserve is cool aloofness of manner, as is ice

explanation.surface: A summer drink order: Pimm's served chilled.
explanation.walkthrough: Pimm's is a British fruit-cup drink of summer; 'ice' here is coldness of manner.
explanation.definitionFit: To save or maintain something unchanged is to hold on to it.

clue.text: Spot of Browning seen in newspaper articles is what holidaymakers may do

indicators.note: seen in places the single letter inside the words around it

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
a and the are the indefinite and definite articles

indicators.note: a spot of something is a little of it, here its first letter

explanation.surface: Getting a bit of a tan is described in the paper's features on holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: B goes between SUN and A, THE. The Sun is a British tabloid daily; 'Browning' looks like the poet but is a tan.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying in sunshine to get a tan is a classic beach holiday activity.

clue.text: Super arsenal initially to play without wings

indicators.note: to play the letters is to rearrange them in a new order
initially means the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Arsenal, a great football team, playing without their wide players.
explanation.walkthrough: SUPER, A and TO are rearranged; 'to' does double duty only on the surface, as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A zoological word for insects lacking flight appendages, from Greek for wingless.

clue.text: Part of the king's speech that might be seen in palace chambers, one's heard

parts.note: things belonging to a monarch are found in a palace

indicators.note: what one hears is the sound of the word, so it is spelt differently

parts.note: chamber pots hold wee, urine

explanation.surface: A phrase in a monarch's address that might be heard in the rooms of a palace.
explanation.walkthrough: Chambers are chamber pots, whose contents are wee, which sounds like WE.
explanation.definitionFit: Monarchs traditionally refer to themselves in the plural, a pronoun used on formal occasions.

clue.text: Heartless stooges from the east increase

indicators.note: in an across clue, from the east means reading from right to left
heartless means the middle letter is taken out

parts.note: puppets are stooges controlled by others

explanation.surface: Cruel henchmen coming from the east and growing in number.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the central P from PUPPETS leaves PUPETS, which 'from the east' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise or intensify something is to boost it.

clue.text: Eastern sages, those with a present? Not half

parts.note: them can mean those, as in them apples

indicators.note: not half means only half of the word is kept

parts.note: a gift is a present

explanation.surface: Wise men from the East bringing gifts, but only half of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' looks like the British phrase meaning 'very much', but here it trims GIFT to GI.
explanation.definitionFit: The three wise men who brought gifts to the infant Jesus came from the East.

clue.text: Hearing that's hard to endure

definitions.meaning: a court hearing is a legal case put to the test
tiresome and wearing, as a very annoying child is

explanation.surface: A court hearing that is hard to sit through.
explanation.definitionFit: A judicial hearing is a case being tried, and something tiresome tests one's patience.

clue.text: Tall and gangling amateur boxing starts from near knockout

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing, so the other piece goes inside

parts.note: lay means non-professional or amateur, as in a lay person

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters

explanation.surface: A tall novice boxer who came close to a knockout.
explanation.walkthrough: N and K, the first letters of 'near' and 'knockout', go inside LAY. 'Boxing' looks like the sport but is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin, tall and awkward in build, with long limbs.

clue.text: Term for "theater" introduced by blue comic before bit of skirt really oozing "it"?

definitions.text: Term for "theater" introduced by blue comic before bit of skirt really oozing "it"?

parts.words: Term for "theater" introduced by blue comic before bit of skirt really oozing "it"?
parts.note: describes a variety show where a risque comedian warms up the crowd before a woman full of sex appeal performs a striptease

explanation.surface: A night at a variety show: a smutty comedian, then a sexy dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' is old slang for sex appeal; 'bit of skirt' is British slang for an attractive woman. The clue describes the show rather than building it.
explanation.definitionFit: A variety entertainment of crude comedy and striptease, especially in American theatres of the early twentieth century.

clue.text: Property in philosophy that's evenly balanced first to last

indicators.note: first to last means the opening letter is moved to the end

parts.note: equal means evenly balanced

explanation.surface: A philosophical property that keeps everything in balance from start to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the E of EQUAL to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Philosophers use this term for a quality as it is subjectively experienced, such as the redness of red.

clue.text: Italian composer involved with Latin castrati

indicators.note: involved means tangled together, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: An Italian composer who worked with Latin texts and castrato singers.
explanation.walkthrough: L and CASTRATI are mixed. Domenico and Alessandro Scarlatti were Italian Baroque composers; castrati sang in operas of that period.
explanation.definitionFit: Alessandro and his son Domenico were Baroque musicians from Italy.

clue.text: Present hostility in Austria and Germany

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the others

parts.note: A is the international vehicle code for Austria
D is the international vehicle code for Germany, from Deutschland
war is open hostility

explanation.surface: Current conflict between two neighbouring European countries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like 'current' but is a verb, to give.
explanation.definitionFit: To present is to give formally, as one does with a prize.

clue.text: Trips emerge tragically for this fisherman

indicators.note: tragically suggests a disaster, so the letters are wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: Fishing trips turn out badly for a fisherman.
explanation.walkthrough: The fisherman is the title character of Benjamin Britten's opera, set on the Suffolk coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Britten's 1945 opera is named after its tragic fishing hero.
